title: A Moon of Uranus May Hide an Ocean 40 Times Deeper Than the Pacific
summary: Imagine an ocean so deep it could swallow the Pacific Ocean 40 times over. That's what scientists think may be hiding inside Ariel, a moon of Uranus. Ariel is only 720 miles across — about the distance from Tucson to Salt Lake City. But long ago, it might have had an ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its icy shell. The Pacific Ocean is only about 2.5 miles deep on average. "Ariel is pretty unique in terms of icy moons," said Alex Patthoff, a scientist who helped study it. How do they know? Ariel's surface is covered in huge cracks and ridges. These cracks could have formed when the moon's insides were squeezed and stretched by Uranus' gravity. That squeezing happens more when a moon's orbit is more oval-shaped. The team used computer models to test this idea. They found Ariel's orbit may once have been much more stretched out — about 40 times more than today. That would have created enough stress to crack the ice. "In order to create those fractures, you have to have either a really thin ice on a really big ocean, or a higher eccentricity and a smaller ocean," Patthoff said. "But either way, we need an ocean." This is the second moon around Uranus that may have had an ocean. Last year, the same team found signs of one under Miranda. "We are finding evidence that the Uranus system may harbor twin ocean worlds," said Tom Nordheim, a scientist at Johns Hopkins University. Scientists still don't know exactly when Ariel's ocean existed or how long it lasted. But they hope a future spacecraft will visit Uranus to find out. "Ultimately, we just need to go back to the Uranus system and see for ourselves," Nordheim said.
why_it_matters: Finding hidden oceans on faraway moons matters because water is one of the key things scientists look for when they ask where life might exist — and it shows how models and computers can help us explore places we cannot visit yet.

background_read: Uranus is a huge, freezing planet made mostly of gas and ice, and it is the seventh planet from the Sun.
In 1986, NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft flew past Uranus and took the only close-up pictures we have of Ariel and its neighbour moons.
Scientists think several icy moons in our solar system hide oceans under their frozen crusts — for example Europa, a moon of Jupiter.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists including Alex Patthoff and Tom Nordheim of Johns Hopkins University, studying the moon Ariel
WHAT: They found evidence that Ariel once had a huge ocean under its icy shell, and that cracks on its surface may have formed when its orbit was more stretched out
WHERE: Ariel, a small moon orbiting the planet Uranus far out in the solar system
WHY: The squeezing and stretching from Uranus' gravity could only crack the ice if there was an ocean underneath, making Ariel a possible ocean world

perspectives.description: They see Ariel as a second possible ocean world around Uranus, which would make the whole Uranus system a much more interesting place to explore.
No spacecraft has been back to Uranus since Voyager 2, so the ocean idea comes only from computer models — it might not be true.
Even if an ocean existed, nobody yet knows when it was there or how long it lasted, and a long-lasting ocean is what life would need.
